questions.q: What is the standard SI unit of speed, and what two base physical quantities are used to derive it?
questions.a: The standard SI unit of speed is meters per second (m/s), derived from the base quantities of length (measured in meters) and time (measured in seconds). A wrong answer often confuses speed with force or energy units, or mistakenly states that kilometers per hour is the official SI unit rather than a convenient everyday unit.

questions.q: Why is it incorrect to state that an object traveling a long distance always has a higher speed than an object traveling a short distance? Explain using the formula for speed.
questions.a: Speed depends on *both* distance and time, not distance alone. If Object A travels 100 meters in 10 seconds (speed = 10 m/s) and Object B travels 50 meters in 2 seconds (speed = 25 m/s), Object B is faster despite covering a shorter distance because it takes much less time. A wrong answer shows a failure to recognize speed as a ratio, focusing only on the numerator (distance) while ignoring the denominator (time).

questions.q: A cyclist travels a distance of 180 meters on a flat road in 30 seconds. Calculate the speed of the cyclist in meters per second (m/s).
questions.a:
Given distance $d = 180\text{ m}$ and time $t = 30\text{ s}$. 
Step 1: Identify the formula: $speed = \frac{distance}{time}$. 
Step 2: Substitute values: $speed = \frac{180\text{ m}}{30\text{ s}}$. 
Step 3: Compute: $180 \div 30 = 6$. 
Step 4: Attach units: $6\text{ m/s}$. 
A wrong answer, such as 5400 m/s (from multiplying distance and time) or 0.16 m/s (from dividing time by distance), indicates confusion over formula placement or arithmetic inversion.

questions.q: Two cars, Car X and Car Y, travel between Mumbai and Pune. Car X covers 150 km in 3 hours, while Car Y covers 200 km in 4 hours. Compare their speeds and determine which car traveled faster.
questions.a: Speed of Car X = $\frac{150\text{ km}}{3\text{ h}} = 50\text{ km/h}$. Speed of Car Y = $\frac{200\text{ km}}{4\text{ h}} = 50\text{ km/h}$. Both cars traveled at the exact same speed. A wrong answer usually assumes Car Y is faster simply because it covered a greater total distance, ignoring the extra time it took.

questions.q: A student calculates the running speed of an ant to be $2500\text{ m/s}$. Evaluate whether this numerical result is physically reasonable, and explain why or why not.
questions.a: This result is entirely unreasonable because $2500\text{ m/s}$ is faster than a fighter jet, whereas ants move very slowly over a fraction of a meter in several seconds. A realistic speed for an ant would be a fraction of a meter per second (e.g., $0.02\text{ m/s}$). A wrong answer shows a lack of physical intuition and failure to check if computational outputs make sense in the real world.

questions.q: Design a simple backyard experiment using a rolling marble, a measuring tape, and a stopwatch to determine the average speed of the marble down an inclined wooden plank.
questions.a: A good answer will state: Set up a wooden plank at an angle, mark a starting point (0 cm) and a finish point (e.g., 200 cm) using the measuring tape. Release the marble and use the stopwatch to record the exact time $t$ in seconds it takes to roll from start to finish. Finally, divide the measured distance by the recorded time to find the average speed in cm/s. A poor answer fails to include measurable parameters, lacks timing tools, or does not mention the formula calculation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The standard ______ (SI) unit of speed is meters per second (m/s), and it measures how fast an object changes its position in a given direction.
Fill in the blank: Observe a school bus ______ down an Indian residential road past a landmark, noting how much ground it covers as a wall clock ticks off seconds.
What is Speed? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: The standard international (SI) unit of speed is meters per second (m/s), and it measures how fast an object changes its position in a given direction.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Speed?
questions.a: Students often confuse the units of speed and add or multiply distance and time values arbitrarily instead of dividing them.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can calculate speed, distance, or time given the other two variables, perform correct unit conversions between km/h and m/s, and explain physical motion from word problems or experimental data.
